                    ### Question
                    A 59-year-old male presents to the emergency room with shortness of breath. Ten days ago, he was in the cardiac critical care unit after receiving a balloon angioplasty and a bare metal stent for an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). On physical examination, a holosystolic murmur is heard at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla. You also detect an S3 and bilateral crackles in the lung bases. What is the most likely etiology of this patient's acute decompensated heart failure?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Rupture of the anterior papillary muscle on the right ventricle
opb. Rupture of the posterior papillary muscle on the right ventricle
opc. Rupture of the septal papillary muscle on the right ventricle
opd. Rupture of the anterolateral papillary muscle of the left ventricle
ope. Rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle of the left ventricle

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely etiology of this patient's acute decompensated heart failure is the rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle of the left ventricle. This is supported by the standard medical consensus that the posteromedial papillary muscle is more prone to rupture following an inferior myocardial infarction due to its single blood supply from the posterior descending artery. The rupture leads to acute mitral regurgitation, which is characterized by a holosystolic murmur at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla, an S3 heart sound, and pulmonary congestion, as evidenced by bilateral crackles. The retrieved evidence path confirms that mitral valve insufficiency causes a pansystolic murmur, which aligns with the clinical findings. The other options involving the right ventricle are less likely, as they would typically result in tricuspid regurgitation, which does not match the described murmur or the acute heart failure presentation.
